lesson.title: Line Graphs: Watching Numbers Tell a Story

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Imagine you plant a sunflower seed in your backyard in Surrey, and every Sunday you measure how tall it is with a metre stick. You write the numbers in a table. The table is neat and tidy, but it's just a row of numbers. It's hard to feel how fast that sunflower is shooting up, isn't it? That's exactly the problem a line graph solves.

visual.caption: Sunflower height in centimetres, measured every Sunday

steps.say: Here is the same sunflower data, but drawn as a line graph. We put the weeks along the bottom and the height in centimetres up the side. Each measurement becomes one dot, and then we join the dots with straight lines. Look at that — the line climbs up, and now you can SEE the sunflower growing. Same numbers, but suddenly they tell a story.

visual.caption: The same table, now as a line graph — the line climbs as the plant grows

steps.say: Let's learn how to build one, step by step. First, draw two lines like a big letter L. The bottom line is for TIME — weeks, hours, months. The side line is for the AMOUNT we measured — centimetres, degrees, dollars. Second, choose a scale for the side line and count up evenly, like ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty. Third, put a dot where each week meets its height. Fourth, join the dots. That's it — four little steps and you have a line graph.

visual.caption: Go up from Week 2, across to 35 — that dot means 35 centimetres

steps.say: Now let's read the graph. Slide your finger to Week 2 and look up — the dot sits at thirty-five centimetres. Now here's the clever part: the STEEPNESS tells you how fast things changed. From Week 1 to Week 2 the plant went from twenty to thirty-five, that's a jump of fifteen centimetres — the steepest climb on the whole graph. But from Week 3 to Week 4 it only went from forty-five to fifty, just five centimetres. The line gets flatter because the sunflower is slowing down. Steep means fast, flat means slow.

visual.caption: Steepest part: Week 1 to Week 2, a 15 cm jump. Flattest: Week 3 to Week 4, only 5 cm

steps.say: Ready for a slightly trickier one? Here's a spring day in Vancouver. Every two hours, we checked the thermometer and wrote down the temperature in degrees Celsius. Look at the table. Can you spot what's different about this data? The numbers go up for a while, and then they come back down. A table like this is hard to picture in your head — so let's graph it.

visual.caption: Temperature in degrees Celsius on a spring day in Vancouver

steps.say: There it is — a hill! The line climbs all morning, reaches its highest point at three in the afternoon at eighteen degrees, and then slides back down as evening comes. From nine in the morning to three in the afternoon, it warmed up from eight to eighteen, that's ten degrees warmer. Then from three to seven in the evening, it dropped from eighteen down to ten, which is eight degrees cooler. A line graph shows you the ups AND the downs, and that's why weather people love them.

visual.caption: Up 10 degrees to the 3 p.m. peak, then down 8 degrees by 7 p.m.

steps.say: One last little secret. Because the dots are joined, you can make a smart guess about the in-between times too. Nobody checked the thermometer at ten in the morning, but the line between eight and twelve passes right around ten degrees — so ten degrees is a very sensible guess. That's what makes line graphs special: they don't just show what you measured, they help you predict what happened in between and what might come next. Beautiful work today!

visual.caption: The line between two dots lets you estimate times you never measured

lesson.answer: A line graph turns a table of numbers into a picture over time — dots joined by lines, where climbing means going up, falling means going down, and steeper means faster.

practice.question: Priya measures the snow depth at Grouse Mountain on the first day of each month: December 40 cm, January 70 cm, February 110 cm, March 85 cm. Draw a line graph of her data. Between which two months did the snow grow the MOST, and by how many centimetres? What happened between February and March?
practice.answer: The snow grew most between January and February: 110 − 70 = 40 cm. Between February and March the line goes DOWN, so the snow melted by 110 − 85 = 25 cm.
